claim: Excitation-inhibition (E:I) imbalance is theorized as an important pathophysiological mechanism in autism.
source: Excitation-inhibition (E:I) imbalance is theorized as an important pathophysiological mechanism in autism.
evidence: This is a statement about existing theory in the field, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Autism affects males more frequently than females.
source: Autism affects males more frequently than females
evidence: This is established knowledge about autism epidemiology.

claim: Sex-related mechanisms (e.g., X-linked genes, androgen hormones) can influence E:I balance.
source: sex-related mechanisms (e.g., X-linked genes, androgen hormones) can influence E:I balance
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and established knowledge in the field.

claim: The Hurst exponent (H) estimated from fMRI BOLD signal can be an index for underlying change in the synaptic E:I ratio.
source: With a combination of in-silico modeling and in-vivo chemogenetic manipulations in mice, we first show that a time-series metric estimated from fMRI BOLD signal, the Hurst exponent (H), can be an index for underlying change in the synaptic E:I ratio.
evidence: This claim is supported by in-silico modeling and in-vivo experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: H is reduced in the medial prefrontal cortex (MPFC) of autistic males but not females.
source: In autism we find that H is reduced, indicating increased excitation, in the medial prefrontal cortex (MPFC) of autistic males but not females.
evidence: This is supported by human rsfMRI data analysis presented in the results.

claim: Increasingly intact MPFC H is associated with heightened ability to behaviorally camouflage social-communicative difficulties in autistic females.
source: Increasingly intact MPFC H is also associated with heightened ability to behaviorally camouflage social-communicative difficulties, but only in autistic females.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between H and camouflaging scores in the human data.

claim: Rubenstein and Merzenich originally suggested that some types of autism may be explained by an E:I imbalance that may lead to hyper-excitability in cortical circuitry and potentially enhanced levels of neuronal noise.
source: Rubenstein and Merzenich originally suggested that some types of autism may be explained by an E:I imbalance that may lead to hyper-excitability in cortical circuitry and potentially enhanced levels of neuronal noise (Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about prior work, supported by citation.

claim: A majority of the literature about E:I balance in autism extends from investigations of prominent single gene mutations associated with autism and the animal model research around these genes.
source: A majority of the literature about E:I balance in autism extends from investigations of prominent single gene mutations associated with autism and the animal model research around these genes (Sohal and Rubenstein, 2019; Nelson and Valakh, 2015).
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature, supported by citations.

claim: Many highly penetrant autism-associated genes are located on the sex chromosomes.
source: Many highly penetrant autism-associated genes are located on the sex chromosomes (e.g., FMR1, MECP2, NLGN3, GABRA3, ARX, SYN1) and are known to lead to pathophysiology implicating E:I dysregulation (Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003; Lee et al., 2017; Bozzi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Genes playing important roles in the balance between excitation and inhibition in the brain (e.g., MEF2C, GRIK2, GRIA1, SCN3A, SCN9A, NPTX2) are highly sensitive to androgens in human neuronal stem cells.
source: Other genes playing important roles in the balance between excitation and inhibition in the brain (e.g., MEF2C, GRIK2, GRIA1, SCN3A, SCN9A, NPTX2) are highly sensitive to androgens in human neuronal stem cells and are highly expressed in 'social brain' circuitry such as the default mode network, and in particular, the medial prefrontal cortex (MPFC) (Lombardo et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation to enhance excitation in mouse MPFC results in changes in social behavior.
source: Optogenetic stimulation to enhance excitation in mouse MPFC also results in changes in social behavior (Yizhar et al., 2011; Selimbeyoglu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Many cognitively able adult autistic women engage in camouflaging behaviors that tend to compensate or mask their social-communicative difficulties moreso than autistic men.
source: It is known that many cognitively able adult autistic women engage in camouflaging behaviors that tend to compensate or mask their social-communicative difficulties moreso than autistic men (Lai et al., 2017b; Hull et al., 2020; Schuck et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Autistic males show reduced ventral MPFC (vMPFC) self-representation response.
source: Prior work has shown that whereas autistic males show reduced ventral MPFC (vMPFC) self-representation response, autistic females show intact vMPFC self-representation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The degree to which vMPFC shows intact self-representation response in autistic females is associated with enhanced ability to camouflage.
source: Furthermore, the degree to which vMPFC shows intact self-representation response in autistic females is associated with enhanced ability to camouflage (Lai et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: LFP and resting state fMRI (rsfMRI) data exhibits rich spectral properties, with power decreasing as function of frequency.
source: It has been long known that LFP and resting state fMRI (rsfMRI) data exhibits rich spectral properties, with power decreasing as function of frequency (Bullmore et al., 2001; Maxim et al., 2005; He, 2011; Bédard et al., 2006; He, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Models of neural networks have reported that the E:I ratio has profound effects on the spectral shape of electrophysiological activity.
source: Models of neural networks have reported that the E:I ratio has profound effects on the spectral shape of electrophysiological activity (Brunel and Wang, 2003; Mazzoni et al., 2008; Lombardi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: The exponent of the 1/f spectral power law, an index closely related to the Hurst exponent (H), reflects the extent of E:I imbalance.
source: Recent work with simplified models has proposed that the exponent of the 1/f spectral power law, an index closely related to the Hurst exponent (H), reflects the extent of E:I imbalance (Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Neurophysiologically heightened E:I ratio generates flatter 1/f slope in LFP data and this could drive H (as measured in BOLD) to be decreased.
source: This suggests that neurophysiologically heightened E:I ratio generates flatter 1/f slope in LFP data and this could drive H (as measured in BOLD) to be decreased.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior work cited.

claim: H is atypically decreased in rsfMRI data of adult autistic males, particularly for social brain areas like MPFC.
source: In past work we have shown that H is atypically decreased in rsfMRI data of adult autistic males, particularly for social brain areas like MPFC (Lai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Lower levels of H can be interpreted as closer to what would be expected of a completely noisy random signal (e.g., white noise produces an H = 0.5).
source: H is statistically relevant for the concept of 'neural noise' since lower levels of H can be interpreted as closer to what would be expected of a completely noisy random signal (e.g., white noise produces an H = 0.5).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the Hurst exponent.

claim: Prior work has shown case-control differences in the intrinsic neural timescale in autism.
source: Related to H and long-memory characteristics of the rsfMRI time-series, prior work has also shown case-control differences in the intrinsic neural timescale in autism (e.g., magnitude of temporal autocorrelation) (Watanabe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the recurrent network model, as E:I ratio increases (by decreasing g), H decreases, but only when g is below the baseline reference value.
source: As expected, H decreases with decreasing g (i.e. increasing E:I ratio), but only when g is below the baseline reference value (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In the recurrent network model, changes in synaptic E:I ratio are reflected by and could be inferred from the overall LFP readout of 1/f slope or H.
source: These results clearly indicate that, in a biologically plausible computational model of local cortical microcircuitry including recurrent connections between excitatory and inhibitory neuronal populations, changes in synaptic E:I ratio are reflected by and thus could be inferred from the overall LFP readout of 1/f slope or H.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling results.

claim: Simulated BOLD from the recurrent model shows that H in BOLD decreases as E:I ratio is shifted toward higher excitation by lowering the value of g with respect to the reference value.
source: Strikingly, H in BOLD shows the same dependency on g as observed in LFP data (Figure 2C-D) - H in BOLD decreases as E:I ratio is shifted toward higher excitation by lowering the value of g with respect to the reference value.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Studies with simultaneous LFP and BOLD measured in animals have shown that BOLD signal correlates more strongly with the LFP than with spikes.
source: Studies with simultaneous LFP and BOLD measured in animals have shown that although BOLD signal correlates with both LFPs and spikes, it correlates more strongly with the LFP than with spikes (Logothetis et al., 2001; Magri et al., 2012; Rauch et al., 2008; Viswanathan and Freeman, 2007; Lauritzen and Gold, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior empirical work.

claim: LFP power shows time-lagged correlations with the time course of BOLD signal and different frequency bands vary in how they correlate with measured BOLD signal.
source: Further studies with simultaneous LFP and BOLD measured in non-human primates (Logothetis et al., 2001; Magri et al., 2012; Schölvinck et al., 2010) have considered the relationship between frequency-resolved LFPs and BOLD and indicate that LFP power shows time-lagged correlations with the time course of BOLD signal and that different frequency bands vary in how they correlate with measured BOLD signal.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior empirical work.

claim: Gamma band frequencies tend to show the strongest correlation between LFP power and BOLD signal.
source: In particular, gamma band frequencies tend to show the strongest correlation between LFP power and BOLD signal.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior empirical work.

claim: Frequency dependency of the EEG-BOLD relationship, with prominent predictive power of the gamma band, is reported in humans.
source: Frequency dependency of the EEG-BOLD relationship, with prominent predictive power of the gamma band, is also reported in humans (Scheeringa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The method for simulating BOLD from recurrent model LFP data retains key empirical relationships observed between real LFP power and BOLD.
source: Thus, our method for simulating BOLD from recurrent model LFP data retains key empirical relationships observed between real LFP power and BOLD.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of simulated data to empirical observations.

claim: In the recurrent model simulation of hM3Dq DREADD manipulation, progressively lowering voltage threshold for spike initiation from -52 to -53 mV resulted in more positive low-frequency and flatter high-frequency 1/f slopes and caused decreases in H.
source: Progressively lowering Vth from -52 to -53 mV resulted in more positive low-frequency and flatter high-frequency 1/f slopes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and also caused decreases in H (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the recurrent model simulation of hM4Di DREADD manipulation, decreasing the resting potential from -70 to -75 mV produced varied effects in 1/f slopes and resulted in a slight increase of H.
source: Decreasing EL from the baseline value of -70 to -75 mV produced varied effects in 1/f slopes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and resulted in a slight increase of H (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In mouse PFC, H is modulated over time by the hM3Dq DREADD excitation manipulation.
source: We find that H is modulated over time by the DREADD manipulation (condition*time*treatment phase interaction F = 349.03, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of in-vivo mouse rsfMRI data.

claim: During the Baseline phase of rsfMRI scanning before the DREADD-actuator CNO was injected, H under DREADD or a SHAM control conditions are not affected.
source: During the Baseline phase of rsfMRI scanning before the DREADD-actuator CNO was injected, H under DREADD or a SHAM control conditions are not affected (condition main effect F = 0.82, p=0.37; condition*time interaction F = 0.36, p=0.54).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of in-vivo mouse rsfMRI data.

claim: During the Transition phase of the hM3Dq DREADD experiment, H drops over time at a steeper rate during the DREADD condition compared to the SHAM condition.
source: However, during the Transition phase of the experiment where the CNO begins to have its effects, we find a condition*time interaction (F = 4.94, p=0.0262), whereby H drops over time at a steeper rate during the DREADD condition compared to the SHAM condition (green line in Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of in-vivo mouse rsfMRI data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: During the Treatment phase of the hM3Dq DREADD experiment, H is reduced in the DREADD vs SHAM condition.
source: Finally, during the Treatment phase of the experiment, where the drug exerts its maximal effect, there is a significant main effect of condition (F = 12.92, p=0.0011) and no condition*time interaction (F = 0.66, p=0.4182) (blue line in Figure 3C) (Table 1). This effect is explained by H being reduced in the DREADD vs SHAM condition.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of in-vivo mouse rsfMRI data shown in Figure 3C and Table 1.

claim: Chemogenetically silencing both excitatory and inhibitory neurons with hM4Di DREADD has no strong main effects of condition or condition*time interactions in any of the baseline, transition, or treatment phases of the experiment.
source: While a significant 3-way interaction between condition, time, and treatment phase was present (F = 85.8, p<0.0001), there were no strong main effects of condition or condition*time interactions in any of the baseline, transition, or treatment phases of the experiment (see Table 2 and Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of in-vivo mouse rsfMRI data shown in Figure 3D and Table 2.

claim: Genes differentially expressed by DHT are highly prominent within the gene set of autism-associated genes that affect excitatory neurons (OR = 1.67, p=0.03).
source: Genes differentially expressed by DHT are highly prominent within the gene set of autism-associated genes that affect excitatory neurons (OR = 1.67, p=0.03), with most of the overlapping genes being those whereby DHT upregulates expression (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis of genomic data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Genes associated with autism that affect inhibitory neuronal cell types or other non-neuronal cells (e.g., microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes) are not enriched for DHT differentially expressed genes.
source: By contrast, genes associated with autism that affect inhibitory neuronal cell types or other non-neuronal cells (e.g., microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes) are not enriched for DHT differentially expressed genes (inhibitory neurons: OR = 1.51, p=0.12; microglia: OR = 0.78, p=0.78; astrocytes or oligodendrocytes: OR = 1.11, p=0.49).
evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis of genomic data.

claim: DHT-sensitive and autism-associated excitatory neuron genes are highly expressed in MPFC, PCC, insula, and intraparietal sulcus in the adult human brain.
source: A one-sample t-test of gene maps from the Allen Institute Human Brain Atlas (Hawrylycz et al., 2012) shows that this subset of DHT-sensitive and autism-associated excitatory neuron genes are highly expressed in MPFC, PCC, insula, and intraparietal sulcus, amongst other areas (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Mass-univariate analysis uncovered one region in ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vMPFC), region p32, with a sex-by-diagnosis interaction passing FDR q < 0.05 (F(5,104) = 15.13, p=0.0001, partial η2 = 0.12).
source: Mass-univariate analysis uncovered one region in ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vMPFC), region p32, with a sex-by-diagnosis interaction passing FDR q < 0.05 (F(5,104) = 15.13, p=0.0001, partial η2 = 0.12) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of human rsfMRI data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The sex-by-diagnosis interaction in vMPFC area p32 is driven by a large TD >Autism effect in males (Cohen's d = 1.30) and a small Autism >TD effect in females (Cohen's d = −0.27).
source: In line with directionality of our predictions, this interaction effect is driven by a large TD >Autism effect in males (Cohen's d = 1.30) and a small Autism >TD effect in females (Cohen's d = −0.27) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by effect size analysis of human rsfMRI data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PLS analysis identified one neural system expressing the sex-by-diagnosis interaction (d = 2.04, p=0.036) that included default mode network (DMN) areas such as MPFC and posterior cingulate cortex/precuneus (PCC).
source: PLS analysis identified one neural system expressing the same sex-by-diagnosis interaction (d = 2.04, p=0.036) and included default mode network (DMN) areas such as MPFC and posterior cingulate cortex/precuneus (PCC) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and other non-DMN areas such as insula, lateral prefrontal cortex, somatosensory and motor cortices, intraparietal sulcus, amongst others (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by PLS analysis of human rsfMRI data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In autistic females, increased camouflaging was strongly associated with increased H in vMPFC (r = 0.60, p=0.001).
source: In autistic females, increased camouflaging was strongly associated with increased H in vMPFC (r = 0.60, p=0.001).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of human rsfMRI and behavioral data.

claim: In autistic males, there is no significant association between camouflaging and H in vMPFC (r = −0.10, p=0.63).
source: However, no significant association was apparent in autistic males (r = −0.10, p=0.63).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of human rsfMRI and behavioral data.

claim: The strength of the brain-behavioral correlation between H and camouflaging significantly differed between autistic males and females (z = 2.58, p=0.009).
source: The strength of this brain-behavioral correlation significantly differed between autistic males and females (z = 2.58, p=0.009) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of correlations shown in Figure 5E.

claim: ADOS social-communication (SC) was negatively correlated with vMPFC H in autistic females (r = −0.51, p=0.008) indicating higher H with lower SC severity.
source: ADOS social-communication (SC) was negatively correlated with vMPFC H in autistic females (r = −0.51, p=0.008) indicating higher H with lower SC severity.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of human rsfMRI and clinical data.

claim: The relationship between ADOS social-communication and vMPFC H was not present in autistic males (r = −0.04, p=0.83).
source: This relationship was not present in autistic males (r = −0.04, p=0.83).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of human rsfMRI and clinical data.

claim: The recurrent network model includes interactions within and between excitatory and inhibitory neuronal populations.
source: Importantly, our approach takes a major step forward from prior work (Gao et al., 2017) by utilizing a model that includes interactions within and between excitatory and inhibitory neuronal populations.
evidence: This is a description of the computational model used in the study.

claim: The recurrent network model is composed of 5000 neurons, of which 4000 are excitatory and 1000 inhibitory.
source: The network is composed of 5000 neurons, of which 4000 are excitatory (i.e. they form AMPA-like excitatory synapses with other neurons) and 1000 inhibitory (forming GABA-like synapses).
evidence: This is a description of the computational model parameters.

claim: In the recurrent network model, neurons are randomly connected with a connection probability between each pair of neurons of 0.2.
source: Neurons are randomly connected with a connection probability between each pair of neurons of 0.2.
evidence: This is a description of the computational model parameters.

claim: The LFP in the recurrent model is computed as the sum of absolute values of AMPA and GABA postsynaptic currents on excitatory cells.
source: The LFP is computed as the sum of absolute values of AMPA and GABA postsynaptic currents on excitatory cells (Mazzoni et al., 2008; Mazzoni et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the computational method with citation support.

claim: The simple estimation of LFPs was shown to capture more than 90% of variance of both experimental data recorded from cortical field potentials and of simulated data from a complex three-dimensional model of the dipoles generated by cortical neurons.
source: This simple estimation of LFPs was shown to capture more than 90% of variance of both experimental data recorded from cortical field potentials and of simulated data from a complex three-dimensional model of the dipoles generated by cortical neurons (Mazzoni et al., 2008; Mazzoni et al., 2015; Barbieri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior validation work.

claim: The relationship between E:I and the spectral slope flattens out for high values of I in the recurrent model.
source: In contrast, we found that the relationship between E:I and the spectral slope flattens out for high values of I.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling results.

claim: Higher recurrent inhibition leads to higher peak frequency of gamma oscillations.
source: This, in our view, may in part arise from the fact that, as shown in studies of recurrent network models (Brunel and Wang, 2003), higher recurrent inhibition leads to higher peak frequency of gamma oscillations (i.e. an increase of power at higher frequencies) thus partly counteracting the low-pass filtering effect of inhibitory currents in the uncoupled model.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior work and current modeling results.

claim: The model to generate BOLD from frequency-resolved LFPs reflects several features of the empirical LFP-BOLD relationship - namely the presence of a particularly strong gamma-BOLD relationship and the fact that a better prediction of the BOLD is obtained from the frequency-resolved LFP than from the wideband LFP.
source: Our simple model to generate BOLD from frequency-resolved LFPs reflect several features of the empirical LFP-BOLD relationship - namely the presence of a particularly strong gamma-BOLD relationship and the fact that a better prediction of the BOLD is obtained from the frequency-resolved LFP than from the wideband LFP.
evidence: This is a characterization of the computational model's properties.

claim: A limitation of the simple model is that it cannot capture the negative relationship between the power of some low-frequency LFP bands and the BOLD amplitude that has been reported in some studies.
source: However, a limitation of our simple model is that, in its present form, it cannot capture the negative relationship between the power of some low-frequency LFP bands and the BOLD amplitude that has been reported in some studies (Schölvinck et al., 2010; Scheeringa et al., 2011; Mukamel et al., 2005; Niessing et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an acknowledged limitation of the computational model.

claim: Enhancement of excitation in mouse MPFC results in measurable changes in BOLD readouts as decreases in H.
source: The present work clearly shows that enhancement of excitation results in measurable changes in BOLD readouts as decreases in H.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in-vivo mouse experiments.

claim: Autism-associated genes that affect excitatory neuronal cell types are enriched for genes that are differentially expressed by DHT in human neuronal stem cells.
source: With regards to how sex-related heterogeneity in E:I imbalance might manifest in autism, we utilized genomics data and found that autism-associated genes that affect excitatory neuronal cell types are enriched for genes that are differentially expressed by DHT in human neuronal stem cells.
evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis of genomic data.

claim: Other cell types such as inhibitory neurons do not express autism-associated genes that are also influenced by DHT.
source: Importantly, other cell types such as inhibitory neurons do not express autism-associated genes that are also influenced by DHT.
evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis of genomic data.

claim: Reduced H in autistic males is compatible with the inference of elevated E:I ratio potentially driven by enhanced excitation.
source: Specifically, we examined whether H differs between adult males and females with and without autism. Mass-univariate analysis highlighted one region in vMPFC which showed a sex-by-diagnosis interaction - that is, H was specifically reduced in adult autistic males, but not in autistic females. Reduced H in autistic males is compatible with the inference of elevated E:I ratio potentially driven by enhanced excitation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the human rsfMRI results in the context of the modeling and mouse experiments.

claim: Progressively more intact vMPFC H in autistic females, which are likely reflective of more intact E:I balance, is associated with better ability to camouflage social-communicative difficulties.
source: Strikingly, here we find a similar sex-by-diagnosis interaction effect in vMPFC H as well as a female-specific correlation with camouflaging - as vMPFC H increases, indicative of a more normative or intact level of E:I balance, camouflaging also increases. This converging set of results suggests that intrinsic mechanisms such as E:I balance may be atypical only in cognitively able autistic males at vMPFC. More intact E:I balance in the vMPFC of autistic females may enable better vMPFC-related function (e.g., self-representation) and thus potentially better enable these individuals to camouflage social-communicative difficulties and cope in social situations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analysis between H and camouflaging in autistic females.

claim: Intact E:I balance in vMPFC of females may be an expression of protective factors that are hypothesized to buffer risk for autism in females.
source: It may also be fruitful to examine how intact E:I balance in vMPFC of females may be an expression of protective factors that are hypothesized to buffer risk for autism in females (Robinson et al., 2013; Werling, 2016).
evidence: This is speculation about the implications of the findings, supported by citations to prior work on protective factors.

claim: Spectral properties of neural time-series data, such as H and 1/f slope, can be utilized in neuroimaging readouts like LFP and BOLD as a biomarker for underlying E:I-relevant mechanisms.
source: In conclusion, we show that spectral properties of neural time-series data, such as H and 1/f slope, can be utilized in neuroimaging readouts like LFP and BOLD as a biomarker for underlying E:I-relevant mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined in-silico, in-vivo, and human data.

claim: H in rsfMRI data is reduced in vMPFC and other DMN areas of adult autistic males, but not females.
source: Finally, in application to humans, we show that H in rsfMRI data is reduced in vMPFC and other DMN areas of adult autistic males, but not females.
evidence: This is supported by human rsfMRI data analysis.

claim: Reduced H is indicative of enhanced excitation and thus points to sex-specific dysregulation of E:I balance in social brain networks of autistic males.
source: Reduced H is indicative of enhanced excitation and thus points to sex-specific dysregulation of E:I balance in social brain networks of autistic males.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the human rsfMRI results in the context of the modeling and mouse experiments.

claim: Male-specific dysregulation of E:I balance may be linked to sex-differential early developmental events such as androgen-upregulation of gene expression for genes that play important roles in excitatory neurons.
source: This male-specific dysregulation of E:I balance may be linked to sex-differential early developmental events such as androgen-upregulation of gene expression for genes that play important roles in excitatory neurons (Lombardo et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is speculation about the developmental mechanisms, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The intact levels of H in females may help facilitate elevated levels of compensation known as camouflaging to cope with daily social-communicative difficulties.
source: The intact levels of H in females may help facilitate elevated levels of compensation known as camouflaging to cope with daily social-communicative difficulties.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between H and camouflaging in autistic females.

claim: This work extends the relevance of the E:I imbalance theory of autism beyond evidence from autism-associated rare genetic variants and specify a larger portion of the autism population whereby these E:I mechanisms may be of critical importance.
source: More generally, this work extends the relevance of the E:I imbalance theory of autism beyond evidence from autism-associated rare genetic variants and specify a larger portion of the autism population whereby these E:I mechanisms may be of critical importance.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the broader implications of the work.

claim: All human participants reported cis-gender identity based on a single item inquiring their birth-assigned sex and another on their identified gender.
source: They all reported cis-gender identity based on a single item inquiring their birth-assigned sex and another on their identified gender.
evidence: This is a description of the participant characteristics.

claim: Groups were not statistically different on age or full-scale IQ (FIQ) on the Wechsler Abbreviated Scales of Intelligence (WASI).
source: Groups were not statistically different on age or full-scale IQ (FIQ) on the Wechsler Abbreviated Scales of Intelligence (WASI) (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparisons shown in Table 3.

claim: The final groups used in all analyses did not statistically differ on age (diagnosis main effect: F(3,106) = 0.03, p=0.85; sex main effect: F(3,106) = 0.14, p=0.70; sex-by-diagnosis interaction: F(3,106) = 0.25, p=0.61).
source: The final groups used in all analyses did not statistically differ on age (diagnosis main effect: F(3,106) = 0.03, p=0.85; sex main effect: F(3,106) = 0.14, p=0.70; sex-by-diagnosis interaction: F(3,106) = 0.25, p=0.61)
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparisons.

claim: The final groups used in all analyses did not statistically differ on FIQ (diagnosis main effect: F(3,106) = 3.38, p=0.07; sex main effect: F(3,106) = 0.48, p=0.48; sex-by-diagnosis interaction: F(3,106) = 2.24, p=0.13).
source: or FIQ (diagnosis main effect: F(3,106) = 3.38, p=0.07; sex main effect: F(3,106) = 0.48, p=0.48; sex-by-diagnosis interaction: F(3,106) = 2.24, p=0.13) (see Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparisons shown in Table 3.

claim: Wavelet denoising method has been shown to mitigate substantial spatial and temporal heterogeneity in motion-related artifact that manifests linearly or non-linearly and can do so without the need for data scrubbing.
source: The wavelet denoising method has been shown to mitigate substantial spatial and temporal heterogeneity in motion-related artifact that manifests linearly or non-linearly and can do so without the need for data scrubbing (Patel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior methodological work.

claim: All groups showed average meanFD of less than 0.2 mm.
source: All groups showed average meanFD of less than 0.2 mm (see Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 3.
